thread.title: Average American Retirement Portfolio - Twenty Percent Better Than Average Retiree

author: The Value Portfolio
title: Average American Retirement Portfolio - Twenty Percent Better Than Average Retiree
text:
The Average American Retirement portfolio is a six-figure retirement portfolio created for Seeking Alpha several years ago. The portfolio was originally created because I realized that the average American doesn’t retire with nearly enough money to actually live their lives. Its goal is to provide investors with steady income without requiring them to sell and use the portfolio’s assets.
The last article in the Average American Retirement portfolio was written a year ago. For investors who want to view the recent changes, those can be seen there.
(Image Source: Retirement - Faculty Funds )
Introduction The premise behind the Average American Retirement portfolio stems from the fact that the average head of household in the United States, aged between 55 and 64, has a mere $100 thousand in savings. At the same time, the average American has a life expectancy of 79. That means that the average person has to live 14 years in retirement on their assets.
For those doing the math, without investing the principal, that means the average family will have just $7140 per year. Someone investing it in something safe like bonds will have closer to $9000 but will have that number decrease every single year. This portfolio will allow retirees to maintain their capital value, while gaining $5000+ in income each year. That way, in the event of an emergency, they still have the $5000 portfolio available.
At the same time, the average American investor can take advantage of the long-term growth trend of the stock market.

Portfolio Discussion Due to the portfolio’s ownership of steady companies, it performed surprisingly well over the past year in a tough market environment and dropped a mere 4% across 2018. At the same time, it is still more than 5% where it started at. This doesn’t count the fact that each year since the portfolio’s creation, we haven’t reinvested dividends.
Instead, we’ve been assuming that all dividends for the year have been used for the retiree’s expenses. In fact, the Average American Retirement portfolio has continued to provide strong cash flow while growing. Here’s a comparison of the Average American Retirement portfolio versus a standard retirement portfolio invested in treasuries.
We will assume you’re withdrawing $5300 from each portfolio per year (the amount of income generated by the Average American Retirement portfolio). We’ll also assume the alternative is investing your portfolio in treasuries at 2% and withdrawing any shortfall.

The above shows the difference between two portfolios providing the exact same amount of cash flow. As can be seen, the traditional 2% portfolio has to withdraw additional money to meet the $5300 income retirement. However, the Average American Retirement portfolio makes more than enough from dividends that it doesn’t need to withdraw.
As a result, the portfolio is safe to accrue along with the rest of the stock market, while providing strong dividend income.
In fact, after 4 years, the Average American Retirement Portfolio’s value of $105,000 is more than 20% better than a standard retirement portfolio value. This is a roughly 5% annual beat, roughly equivalent to the amount of money being withdrawn. In other words, you could have almost doubled your withdrawal rate from the Average American Retirement portfolio to be at the same spot as a standard portfolio.
Another hallmark of the Average American Retirement portfolio is I have consistently changed it to prepare for changing market conditions. For example, a year ago, I sold off the portfolio’s position in Apple ( AAPL ). I felt that the company was getting overvalued. Similarly, I plan to readjust the portfolio in this article to reduce the risk. Due to tariffs and changing Fed policies, many groups see an economic slowdown in 2019.
To handle the risk, I plan to move away some from individual companies in the portfolio and move through paying funds. To do this, I will see 136 shares of Aflac. This will provide the portfolio with $6198 worth of capital that can be reinvested. I plan to invest this money into Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) stock. The company’s current dividend means $271 per share in dividends, double what Aflac was paying.
Qualcomm remains in an incredibly strong financial situation. The company has guided from a decrease in sequential revenue due to its lawsuit with Apple; however, Qualcomm appears to be making some blows in the battle. The company has recently won against iPhones being sold in both Germany and China, and will be beating Intel ( INTC ) (Apple’s current modem supplier) to 5G technology.
The lawsuit has already followed significant unpaid dues, and Apple currently owes Qualcomm $7 billion (>10% of Qualcomm market cap). The company still anticipates diluted EPS of $1.1 for the quarter, which comes out to a low-double digit P/E ratio. At the same time, the company plans to continue reducing its share count, buying back tens of millions of shares over the quarter.
Qualcomm still has roughly $8 billion left on its buyback allowance, equivalent to almost 20% of its outstanding shares. That’d save the company $350 million in annual dividend expenses, while enabling it to reward shareholders significantly.
To me, this shows the potential for continued strong dividend from Qualcomm, along with a minimum risk in stock price dropping from continued buyback support. This stock will help provide growing dividend income for our retirees, while exposing them to the technology sector and providing continued long-term growth.
Conclusion The Average American Retirement portfolio has continued to improve on its mandate. The portfolio has increased 5% since its inception, while providing investors more than 5% in annual income. That means the portfolio now beats what a standard retirement portfolio invested in U.S. treasures would have done by 20%. That impressive performance is solid.
The Average American Retirement portfolio was started to help the average retiree who doesn’t have enough savings. The portfolio has performed well, and I have readjusted it for what I believe to be a riskier market in 2019. I look forward to hearing what you guys think about the portfolio below.
